‘Coyote Vs. Acme’s’ cinematic debut is a victory against corporate greed

A ‘Looney Tunes’ comedy that came back from the shelf
James Michael Counts, MOVE Reporter
September 2, 2026
Violet Newton /The Maneater
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:03
Instaread

Studios across Hollywood spend millions of dollars on blockbuster films, and occasionally pay millions more to bury them for tax relief. 2026’s “Coyote vs. Acme” holds the bizarre distinction of suffering both fates.

In 1990, a satirical short story by Ian Frazier was published in The New Yorker titled “Coyote v. Acme.” This story sparked an idea for a “Looney Tunes” comedy of the same nature: Wile E. Coyote would collaborate with lawyers and finally take the corrupt corporation responsible for all his faulty schemes to civil court.

This creative premise lingered until 2015, when future DC Studios leader James Gunn spearheaded an effort to bring the idea to life. After years of production, the film, which shares its title with the short story, wrapped filming in 2022 under director Dave Green. Will Forte stars as a small-town lawyer, and John Cena as the powerful antagonist. Coyote’s big film was set to release on July 21, 2023, which ended up being the date Greta Gerwig’s “Barbie” was released.

In 2023, the film had exclusive audience test screenings, from which this comedic court drama received an overwhelmingly positive response. Christopher Miller, a director of many successful comedies like “The Lego Movie,” claimed it was “funny, charming” and had “good physical comedy timing, with a surprising amount of heart.”

In November of that year, with the movie completed and ready for release, Warner Bros. Pictures announced it would shelve it for financial reasons. It was used as a tax write-off; a familiar move done by Warner Bros.’s new CEO, David Zaslav, as part of a larger campaign to cut costs and save the company $3 billion. It is essentially building a house and then burning it down for the insurance money. The same treatment was given to the already completed “Batgirl” movie the year prior.

However, the public did not share Zaslav’s satisfaction. Social media lashed out at the company, calling it greedy and unappreciative of the art they finance. Director Dave Green shared his heartbreak over the news, stating, “We were all upended by the news that ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ has been shelved.” Lead actor Forte echoed the frustration, acknowledging that despite glowing test scores, the film wasn’t released. “At the end of the day, the people who paid for this movie can obviously do whatever they want with it,” said Forte.

After years of backlash, Warner Bros. decided to put the movie up for sale to other producers for $50 million. Eventually, on March 31, 2025, a small independent company called Ketchup Entertainment took it off their hands. Finally, “Coyote vs. Acme” would be released in cinemas on Aug. 28, 2026.

Audiences were excited to see if this movie would live up to its previous acclaim, and to Warner Bros.’ dismay, it exceeded expectations. It debuted with an outstanding 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, and audiences praised its creative live-action animation hybrid style and its iconic “Looney Tunes” slapstick comedy. While it is far from perfect, its premise is genius, and it is executed in a satisfying and heartwarming way. It is a great watch for kids, “Looney Tunes” fans, and even those not as familiar but who love a good laugh.

Despite its opening weekend generating $15 million, the film’s financial standing isn’t looking great. They paid $50 million for the rights and even more for marketing. For this movie to be profitable, its subsequent weeks will need to do a lot of heavy lifting.

Ironically, the film’s David-versus-Goliath courtroom premise is very similar to the real-world controversy it faced to get onto the big screen. The often-ignored film community had to fight Warner Bros. just to get an already completed movie released. This movie is great enough to watch in cinemas, and if enough people follow suit, Warner Bros. will be unable to avoid its mistake and error in its practices.

“Coyote vs. Acme” stands as a rare victory for moviegoers, but unless the studio learns from this, its near-extinction remains a dangerous precedent for the future of film.
